title: The Guru becomes the disciple
hookLine: he asks the five to initiate him too; men take the name Singh and women Kaur
carry: wonderful the guru, wonderful the disciple

lines: A TEACHER WHO ASKS TO BE GRADED.
cards: Vaisakhi, 1699. The Guru has just given amrit to the five beloved. They stand before him, newly initiated.
Then he does something unexpected. He kneels in front of them, and asks them to give it to him. A teacher who asks the class to grade her.
A coach who runs the same drills as the team. A boss who hands the keys to the newest hire and says: now you lead, and I'll follow. It doesn't happen often.

teach.b: Khalsa is the word the Guru gave to this new community of the initiated.
It comes through Persian from an Arabic root meaning pure, and in the Mughal world it had a precise meaning: land that belonged directly to the ruler, with no middleman in between.
So the Khalsa is pure, and it belongs directly to God, with no one standing in the middle. Now watch the Guru.

teach.h: THE GURU ASKS THE FIVE FOR AMRIT.
teach.b: He asks the five to initiate him in exactly the same way, from the same bowl, and he receives the amrit from their hands. He had been Gobind Rai. From that day he was Gobind Singh.

teach.h: SINGH, A LION. KAUR, A PRINCESS.
teach.b: The men of the Khalsa took the name Singh, meaning lion. The women took the name Kaur, often explained as princess. A Sikh name no longer told the world your caste or your family's trade.
It told them you were a lion, or a princess, in the Guru's family. A Sikh poet remembered as Bhai Gurdas the second later put the moment into a line Sikhs often quote.

teach.h: HIMSELF THE GURU, HIMSELF THE DISCIPLE.
teach.b: In plain words: wonderful, wonderful is Gobind Singh, who is himself the Guru and himself the disciple. The one who teaches bows to the ones he has taught.

teach.h: WONDERFUL THE GURU, WONDERFUL THE DISCIPLE.
teach.b: The Guru sets himself inside the community, not above it. Tradition says that day the Khalsa was also given its outward form, the five articles Sikhs keep, starting with uncut hair. That's a story for later in the path.

how: Initiated Sikhs are members of the Khalsa; Sikh men commonly take the name Singh and Sikh women Kaur, and Guru Gobind Singh's receiving amrit from the Panj Pyare is remembered at every Vaisakhi.

o: the initiated Sikh community, belonging to God
the Sikh word for a local congregation

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.

s: the Guru gave amrit but never took it himself
he asked the five to initiate him, from the same bowl.
Singh and Kaur replaced names that showed caste
a Sikh name no longer told the world your caste or trade.
in the Mughal world, khalsa land had many middlemen
it was land held directly by the ruler, with no middleman.

games.q: you're the Guru. you've just initiated the five beloved. what do you do next?
o: bless them and send them home.
kneel and ask them to initiate you.
appoint one of them as your deputy.
games.why: he asked the five to give him amrit too: himself the Guru, himself the disciple.

practice: Think of someone you teach, lead, raise or look after: a child, a student, a new coworker, a younger sibling. Picture their face, and one thing they've taught you, maybe without knowing it: patience, a new word, a way of seeing.
In your mind, bow to them, the way the Guru knelt before the five.

wordCard.voice: Khalsa. The community of initiated Sikhs founded in 1699, from a word meaning pure, belonging directly to God.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi, from Persian and Arabic: pure; land held directly by the sovereign.

carryVoice: Your line: wonderful the guru, wonderful the disciple. The Guru knelt, and drank from the same bowl. That's eighty-seven.

sources.ref: Bhai Gurdas II (Bhai Gurdas Singh), Var 41 ('vah vah Gobind Singh ape gur chela')
